error, we conclude that the states have established a substantial likelihood 
that DAPA would not genuinely leave the agency and its employees free to 
exercise discretion. * * *
[Although the district court had enjoined DAPA solely on the basis of 
the procedural APA claim, the Fifth Circuit also decided, “as an alternate 
and additional ground” for finding a likelihood of success on the merits, 
that DAPA was inconsistent with the Immigration and Nationality Act. 
The Fifth Circuit then found that the state plaintiffs had satisfied the other 
requirements for a preliminary injunction and affirmed the district court’s 
decision to grant one.]
Kin g , Cir c u it  Ju d g e , Dissenting.
* * * As the majority admits, the [DAPA] Memorandum “facially 
purports to confer discretion.” But the district court ignored this clear 
language, concluding that agency officials implementing DAPA will defy 
the Memorandum and simply rubberstamp applications. * * * For the 
i 
reasons set out below, I would hold that the Memorandum is nothing more
e 
than a general statement of policy and that the district court’s findings
cannot stand, even under clear error review. * * *
• 
* * * “[C]lear error exists when this court is left with the definite and
} 
firm conviction that a mistake has been made.” Ogden v. Comm’r, 244 F.3d
970, 971 (Sth Cir.2001) (per curiam). I am left with such a conviction for 
three independent reasons: (1) the record lacks any probative evidence of 
DAPA’s implementation; (2) the district court erroneously equated DAPA 
with DACA; and (3) even assuming DAPA and DACA can be equated, the 
evidence of DACA’s implementation fails to establish pretext.
It is true that the plain language of the Memorandum—^which, in the 
majority’s words, “facially purports to confer discretion”—may not be 
conclusive if rebutted by “what the agency does in fact.” Profls & 
Patients, 56 F.3d at 596. Here, however, there is no such evidence of what 
the agency has done “in fact,” as DAPA has yet to be implemented. * * *
How, then, did the district court reach the conclusion that the DAPA 
Memorandum’s express inclusion of case-by-case discretion is “merely 
pretext”? * * *
Lacking any probative evidence as to DAPA’s implementation, the 
district court relied most heavily on evidence of DACA’s implementation— 
concluding unequivocally that DAPA will be “implemented exactly like 
DACA.” It is this analysis that the majority finds convincing, all the while
states requested one if the “new declarations create a fact dispute of material consequence to the 
motion.” No such hearing was held, and the court cited the Pahnkas declaration favorably, yet 
described other sources as providing insufficient detail.
